transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2025-08-14
- Time: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: 42 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood), Liam Chen (Redwood), Jordan Rivera (Redwood), Sofia Ramos (BrightWave), Ethan Cole (BrightWave), Rhea Das (BrightWave)

Summary (auto): quick intro, BrightWave background, how they used Redwood, measurable results, marketing outcomes and next steps to publish a case study and podcast episode.

00:00 Ethan: All right welcome back to the BrightWave podcast this week we have some folks from Redwood Inference, welcome Maya and Liam.
00:12 Maya: Thanks so much for having us, um, it's great to be here. I'm Maya, account lead, and we, we worked with Sofia and the team on their personalization rollout.
00:20 Liam: Hi all, Liam from product marketing, excited to dig into the numbers and the story.
00:27 Ethan: Sofia maybe give a quick primer on BrightWave for listeners.
00:31 Sofia: Yeah sure, BrightWave is a mid-size content platform, we do personalized newsletters, dynamic landing pages, and we've been experimenting with LLMs to generate subject lines and content variants at scale. We started this project because open models were too slow and too inconsistent for our SLA, uh, and cost started to climb.
01:02 Jordan: (quiet) so the intro, uh-huh.
01:06 Maya: One thing we heard early on was latency—your users can't wait for a generation step when they're loading a page—so we suggested a Dedicated setup with caching and a smaller context window for subject lines.
01:18 Sofia: Right, and the Redwood team helped with the config—there were a couple of times we were like wait what is KV cache vs prefix caching—so the SE was helpful explaining how it preserves responses across similar prompts.
01:32 Ethan: Did you benchmark before switching to Redwood?
01:35 Sofia: Yeah we did some internal A/Bs, and we also ran a tiny poc where we compared hosted endpoints from other vendors and our own on-prem cluster. The other vendors had good latency on short prompts but throughput dropped when we scaled. On-prem was cheaper per token but we hit reliability issues and patching pain, so that pushed us to look at Redwood dedicated.
02:05 Liam: We also recommended a quantized model variant for the heavy batch runs—saved a lot on GPU and still kept quality acceptable. There was a tradeoff but you could see token cost drop 40% in some runs.
02:20 Sofia: Yeah we saw like 35 to 45% lower cost on average after tuning batching and switching to the 8-bit profile.
02:30 Ethan: Nice, listeners love numbers. Can you share a specific story where performance made a difference?
02:36 Sofia: Sure, during a big product launch we had to generate 120k personalized subject lines within 15 minutes. Our previous setup timed out on about 12% of the queue, which meant losing customers. With Redwood Dedicated and the autoscaling config, we hit the window and timeouts dropped to near zero, so open rates actually increased by about 3.2 percentage points that week.
03:05 Rhea: And the team loved that the console showed per-route cost breakdowns—helped us decide to cache repeated prefixes for weekly digests.
03:15 Maya: There's always that moment where marketing asks for 100 variants and engineering says no way, right? Redwood's batching and cache suggestions let you do more without blowing the budget.
03:26 Ethan: Any hiccups during the rollout?
03:29 Sofia: Uh yes, initially our SSO wasn't mapping groups correctly so some developers couldn't access the private cluster. That was on us and a little on the config; Redwood support jumped on a call same-day and we got it sorted. It wasn't a huge blocker but worth mentioning for other teams.
03:47 Liam: And from a security lens, we set up KMS encryption and audit logs per your compliance needs—Sofia's team required SOC2-style retention and the private deployment path fit nicely.
04:02 Sofia: Yeah we did review the security docs and they were thorough, though some of the acronyms in the doc were, like, a little off? I think the SRE spelled KV cache as K-V space cache once in the doc, but the engineer clarified later.
04:17 Ethan: (laughs) typos make the world go round.
04:20 Jordan: Quick aside, do you still run any models in-house?
04:24 Sofia: We kept a small on-prem failover for very sensitive PII flows, but most of the heavy lifting moved to Redwood where monitoring and rollouts were easier.
04:34 Ethan: Did you use Redwood's rollout features for model updates?
04:37 Sofia: Yes, canary deploys were huge—we pushed a smaller percentage, looked at quality metrics, then widened the rollout. Saved us from a bad regression once.
04:47 Liam: We also hooked quality monitoring to your prompt benchmark suite so alerts triggered if performance dropped below a threshold for key prompts.
04:55 Rhea: About the podcast angle—what did you see from a marketing lift or PR perspective?
04:59 Sofia: A/B-ing subject lines improved CTRs and our paid channel echo was better, so the marketing team could attribute a small but significant revenue bump. We quoted a 1.8% uplift in conversions for the campaign that used Redwood-driven personalization.
05:17 Ethan: That's great. Any specific line or prompt that just killed it?
05:21 Sofia: Honestly it was a micro-prompt tweak, adding in a user preference token, so you could do 'Hey [name], here's a pick just for you based on your likes'—simple but felt personal.
05:33 Maya: Love that—product teams often under-estimate the power of small prompt changes.
05:37 Ethan: Let's talk about cost—listeners always ask how much this costs. Without exacts, can you ballpark the delta versus your previous stack?
05:45 Sofia: Ballpark, we cut our per-variant cost by about 40% after quantization and batching, though there was an initial uplift from Dedicated reservation commitments. Over the quarter we netted savings once utilization leveled up.
06:05 Liam: That's where the reserved capacity math matters. If you have predictable batch windows, Dedicated is usually cheaper. If you're spiky, hosted with burst is sometimes better.
06:16 Ethan: Did you run into any vendor lock-in concerns?
06:19 Sofia: We worried about that—Redwood helped by documenting the model variants and providing an exportable config, and we kept a small failover to avoid full lock-in. The support around model compatibility gave us confidence.
06:32 Maya: One note, we also helped with prompt tests to make sure the quantized variant matched the float variant for your critical prompts. There were a couple of edge cases we adjusted for.
06:42 Ethan: Favorite part of working with Redwood?
06:44 Sofia: The transparency—seeing per-route latency and cost made it easy to argue for investment to execs.
06:52 Rhea: Also the console screenshots were handy for our Martech deck.
06:56 Jordan: Any regrets or things you'd change?
06:58 Sofia: We'd have involved marketing earlier—initially it felt like an engineering project, and marketing's voice could have guided prompt design faster. Next time we'll include campaign writers from day one.
07:12 Liam: Good lesson.
07:14 Ethan: Okay let's do a short lightning round—what's one tip for teams trying to do this?
07:18 Sofia: Start with a small set of high-impact prompts and measure hard.
07:21 Maya: Use batching and caching, but monitor quality closely.
07:24 Liam: Try quantized variants in a canary before full rollout.
07:28 Ethan: Awesome. We'll do a quick closing—what are next steps?
07:31 Maya: We'll send the raw audio and the rough transcript, and Liam will put together a first-draft case study.
07:37 Sofia: We'll provide the usage metrics and sign off on quotes.
07:41 Ethan: Great. Thanks everyone for joining—this was super helpful.
07:45 Maya: Thanks for hosting.
